item.title: Early State Exclusion for 5×5 Jacobi Matrices
item.description:
Pay dirt theory — A 5×5 persymmetric Jacobi matrix with centered spectrum {c−x,c−y,c,c+y,c+x} realizing perfect state transfer lacks early state exclusion if and only if x is an integer multiple of y. Any prescribed even number 2k of early state exclusions can be generated by setting positive eigenvalues y=2k+1 and x=2k+2.

Grade 0.376 · 2.3σ above the day's baseline · matched “quantum chemistry and electronic structure on quantum computers” · Jasmin G. Enriquez, Anastasiia Minenkova

Figure

State overlap |⟨e−iJt𝐞0,𝐞0⟩| versus time t showing multiple zeros (early state exclusions) prior to perfect state transfer at t=π when x is not an integer multiple of y.

Asks

Can early state exclusion occur in a 1D quantum spin chain of 5 qubits that realizes perfect state transfer?

Before

Early state exclusion was proven impossible for 3 qubits and constructed for all even numbers of qubits, but remained open for all odd numbers n>4.

But

Applies strictly to 5×5 Jacobi matrices with centered or symmetric spectra and nearest-neighbor interactions; odd qubit counts n≥7 remain unproven.

Tools

Sylvester formula · Jacobi matrix reconstruction · persymmetric matrix eigentheory · Intermediate Value Theorem

Abstract

In this paper, we present a problem that arose from quantum computing, when the quantum state to be transferred completely vanishes before the first occurrence of the perfect state transfer. It was posed as an open problem for 1D quantum chains with n of qubits, where n>4 is an odd number. We present the solution for n=5. The proofs are accessible to students who studied trigonometry and calculus. As for the set-up the knowledge of eigentheory and inner products from linear algebra is needed.

item.title: Classical phase unwrapping enables large-time-step unitary quantum Krylov subspace diagonalization
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Classical unwrapping post-processing recovers aliased unitary quantum Krylov subspace diagonalization energies with errors ≤1.1×10−7 Ha noiseless, and median errors within chemical accuracy under Gaussian noise σ=10−4 using small Krylov dimensions M=20--65.

Grade 0.367 · 2.2σ above the day's baseline · matched “Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance” · Tushar Kumar Jain, Rahul Maitra, Nicholas J. Mayhall

Figure

Median energy error under Gaussian noise σ=10−4 versus time step τ for ground and first excited states across six molecules. Plain UQKSD fails once aliasing begins, whereas CURE-QKSD maintains chemical accuracy deep into the aliased regime.

Asks

Can energy aliasing from large time steps in unitary quantum Krylov subspace diagonalization be robustly corrected via classical post-processing to avoid numerical ill-conditioning?

Before

Uncorrected principal-branch UQKSD at these aliased time steps gave errors of 0.7--115 Ha, or required small unaliased time steps yielding ill-conditioned overlap matrices.

But

Target energies must fall within classical window; phantom peaks from two colliding states are not excluded; no formal error bounds.

Tools

unitary quantum Krylov subspace diagonalization (UQKSD) · CURE-QKSD phase unwrapping · generalized eigenvalue problem · classical energy windows (CCSD / Hartree-Fock)

Abstract

For computing molecular energies on early fault-tolerant hardware, unitary quantum Krylov subspace diagonalization (UQKSD) avoids both the deep circuits of quantum phase estimation and the Pauli-term sampling of variational methods by extracting the energies from a projected real-time propagator. At a small time step τ, nearly linearly dependent Krylov vectors make the overlap matrix ill-conditioned. Our tests at fixed total evolution time show that additional Krylov vectors then add no accuracy, while the thresholded energy becomes increasingly sensitive to the choice of cutoff. A larger time step improves the conditioning and reduces the Krylov dimension M needed for a target accuracy, but the energies are then known only modulo 2π/τ. We present Classical Unwrapping for Resolving Eigenvalues (CURE-QKSD), a classical post-processing method that leaves the UQKSD circuits and generalized eigenvalue problem unchanged and recovers the missing multiples of 2π/τ from phase-consistency landscapes of one or, when needed, two UQKSD runs. In noiseless tests on six molecules with 12--20 qubits, all 28 targeted energies are recovered in their aliased regimes with final errors of at most 1.1×10⁻⁷~Ha. Under Gaussian noise with σ=10⁻⁴, the median error of the ground or first excited state reaches chemical accuracy at large aliased time steps with M=20--65, whereas uncorrected principal-branch energies are off by 0.7--115~Ha. CURE-QKSD therefore makes aliased time steps usable for UQKSD calculations with smaller, better-conditioned Krylov bases.

item.title: Correlations carried and controlled by coupled non-Markovian environments
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Extends the hierarchy of pure states (HOPS) to communicating non-Markovian environments with photon hopping, establishing that continuous monitoring and local feedback on interior cavities generate and enhance entanglement and correlations between unactuated endpoint spins.

Grade 0.366 · 2.2σ above the day's baseline · matched “Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator” · Stuart Flannigan

Figure

Homodyne measurement of the central cavity and feedback driving only the central spin increases endpoint spin-spin correlations (zz and yy) and endpoint concurrence over time across a three-cavity chain.

Asks

How can quantum systems coupled to spatially communicating, non-Markovian environments be simulated and controlled using local hierarchy methods?

But

Numerical truncation of hierarchy depth KH, Gaussian non-Markovian bosonic environments, zero-temperature initial bath vacuum.

Tools

Correlated hierarchy of pure states (HOPS) · Non-Markovian quantum state diffusion · Continuous homodyne measurement and feedback · Matrix product states (MPS)

Code. https://github.com/SFlann/correlated-hops

Abstract

An environment can retain quantum information and carry it between spatially separated systems. Describing the combined influence of these processes requires a treatment of both environmental memory and spatial correlations. Here, we formulate a local hierarchy of pure states for quantum systems coupled to spatially correlated, non-Markovian environments whose modes themselves exchange excitations. We use this method to describe the reduced spin dynamics of a chain of locally coupled Rabi spin--cavity pairs motivated by cavity-QED implementations, where photon hopping in the eliminated cavity environment generates correlations and entanglement between otherwise isolated spins. Monitoring intermediate cavities and feeding their measurement records back onto the corresponding spins further enhances correlations between endpoint spins that receive no direct feedback. The delayed response when feedback starts, and continued entanglement growth after it stops, support a mechanism in which coherent environmental dynamics carry the effects of earlier feedback to the endpoint spins. Finally, tensor-network simulations of XXZ and Heisenberg chains show how environmental transport changes many-body correlation patterns. These results show how coupled environments and local feedback can control correlations between distant spins. We provide a numerically exact stochastic pure-state framework for simulating these processes, opening up avenues to explore the coherent and dissipative control of interacting non-Markovian many-body systems.

item.title: Cross-Platform Benchmarking of GHZ-State Generation in Quantum Processors via Cloud Services
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Large superconducting quantum processors (107 to 156 qubits) support GHZ states passing genuine multipartite entanglement non-exclusion criteria on at most N∗=27 and N∗=24 qubits (<23% of register), whereas a 12-qubit trapped-ion processor passes on its full register (N∗=12). Under a strict GME certification rule, only four of nine commercial processors succeed at any tested size.

Grade 0.354 · 2.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance” · Sergio Hernández, Unai Aseguinolaza, David Aguirre, Marta Gili, Joseba Hernández, Guillermo Valverde, Uxue Ballarin Manso, Uxue Auzmendi, Iker Pastor, Pablo García Bringas, Ane Blázquez García, Rubén Peña, Mikel Sanz

Figure

Comparison of largest passing GHZ size N∗ against total physical qubits Ntot, alongside register utilization ratios and per-qubit GHZ error rates across nine processors.

Asks

How do commercial cloud-accessible quantum computing platforms across different hardware modalities compare when preparing genuine multipartite entangled GHZ states under standard end-user compilation?

But

Default provider compilations without error mitigation; stabilizer sample size set by ε=δ=0.10; evaluations limited to single runs or sparse binary-searched register sizes.

Tools

QuSquare benchmark suite · Direct Fidelity Estimation (DFE) · remote cloud-access APIs (Amazon Braket, Qiskit Runtime) · superconducting and trapped-ion QPUs

Code. https://github.com/NQUIRE-Center/Cross-Platform-Benchmarking/tree/main/GHZ-State_Generation

Abstract

Quantum computing has rapidly evolved into a diverse ecosystem of hardware platforms that differ in their underlying technologies and operational characteristics. Consequently, benchmarking has become essential for identifying the strengths of quantum processors, comparing their performance, and enabling informed decisions when selecting the most appropriate quantum computing platform for specific applications. In this work, we benchmark nine commercially accessible quantum processors from five vendors, spanning superconducting and trapped-ion technologies, using the multipartite entanglement benchmark from the QuSquare suite. All experiments were performed through remote cloud-access services, with the default compilation of each provider and without error mitigation, reflecting the performance experienced by end users. The benchmark estimates the fidelity of Greenberger--Horne--Zeilinger (GHZ) states by direct fidelity estimation and searches for the largest GHZ state whose fidelity is compatible, within the statistical error, with the genuine multipartite entanglement (GME) threshold F=1/2. Our results reveal a substantial gap between the total number of physical qubits available on a processor and the size of the largest GHZ state passing the benchmark: the best superconducting processors reach N^*=27 and N^*=24 qubits, less than a quarter of their registers, whereas the 12-qubit trapped-ion processor passes with its full register. We further show that median calibration data are poor predictors of the benchmark outcome, and that the reported sizes depend strongly on the statistical decision rule: requiring certified GME reduces the number of devices that succeed at any tested size from nine to four. These results provide a baseline for future cross-platform benchmarking of quantum processors.

item.title: Quantum simulation of real-time bosonic dynamics with binary and unary position encodings on superconducting and trapped-ion processors
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Unary position encoding compressed into fixed-size circuits of about 200 two-qubit gates resolves double-well tunneling, dropping right-well probability from 0.97 to 0.06 on IBM Phoenix and 0.96 to 0.12 on IonQ Forte. Binary product formulas require several thousand two-qubit gates and fail to show population transfer.

Grade 0.352 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “analog quantum simulation of lattice models on cold atoms or superconducting ar…” · Masanori Hanada, Jiwoo Seo, Seok-Kyun Son, Junggi Yoon

Figure

Position probability distributions versus coordinate x and time t for 14-site unary double-well dynamics. Both IBM Phoenix and IonQ Forte capture the coherent wave-packet tunneling from the right well to the left well, matching exact-grid and ideal product-formula baselines.

Asks

Can real-time bosonic dynamics discretized on a position lattice be simulated faithfully on noisy quantum hardware using binary versus unary encodings?

But

Post-selected on single-excitation code space. Exact fixed-size circuit compression holds only for single degrees of freedom; inter-register interactions prevent exact compression in coupled-oscillator systems.

Tools

IBM Phoenix (Nighthawk r2) · IonQ Forte (forte-1) · Givens-rotation circuit compression · single-excitation subspace post-selection

Abstract

Simulating a bosonic degree of freedom on qubit hardware requires discretizing its position space, and the qubit encoding of the resulting lattice determines the circuits that realize its real-time dynamics. We compare binary and unary encodings of a position lattice on superconducting (IBM) and trapped-ion (IonQ) processors. Binary encoding applies the kinetic term through the quantum Fourier transform; unary encoding uses one qubit per site, single-qubit rotations for the potential and excitation-conserving exchange gates for the kinetic term. For a single degree of freedom the unary dynamics is a free-fermion problem, and its product formula compresses exactly into a nearest-neighbor circuit of fixed size. With about two hundred two-qubit gates, these circuits resolve tunneling in a symmetric double well on both processors, with the right-well probability falling from 0.97 to 0.06 on IBM and from 0.96 to 0.12 on IonQ, whereas binary product-formula circuits with several thousand two-qubit gates do not reproduce the transfer. Noiseless emulation indicates that this contrast reflects the compilation as well as the encoding: without the fixed-size optimization, a unary product formula that captures the transfer also requires several thousand two-qubit gates. Post-selection on the single-excitation subspace removes leakage, and because every energy eigenstate of the symmetric grid populates both wells equally, the measured population reversal bounds the coherence between energy eigenstates from below. Coupled-oscillator benchmarks, where inter-register interactions prevent this exact compression, show that the preferred encoding depends on the grid size and the evolution time.

item.title: A Hardware-Trained Generative Quantum Eigensolver for Sample-Based Quantum Diagonalization of Organotin Hydroxides up to 70 Qubits
item.description:
Worth a look new result — GQE transformer policy trained directly on a 70-qubit processor generates state-preparation circuits that recover energies within 15 mHa of DMRG across 27 of 28 test runs (median 4.5 mHa). Circuits at 56–70 qubits require 34–72 times fewer two-qubit gates than transpiled LUCJ ansätze.

Grade 0.346 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “Probing many-body dynamics on a 51-atom quantum simulator” · Kunal Kumar, Kimberlee Keithley, Toshiya Iwamori, Shu Kanno, Ikko Hamamura, Takao Kobayashi, Akira Koseki, Qi Gao, Naoki Yamamoto, Hiroshi Horii, Yuri Kobayashi, Borja Peropadre, Kouhei Nakaji, Toru Imai, Takayuki Osogami

Figure

Excitation distribution (HF, single, double, triple, quadruple, higher) plotted across 10 sampled circuits for eleven organotin molecules from 32 to 70 qubits, showing physical shot spread across excitation manifolds without collapsing to Hartree–Fock.

Asks

Can generative quantum eigensolver policies be trained directly with quantum hardware feedback at active spaces up to 70 qubits beyond exact classical simulation?

But

Single training run per lineage. Evaluated on 10 sampled circuits per molecule with up to 100,000 shots per circuit; subspace recovery capped at 20,000 strings.

Tools

generative quantum eigensolver (GQE) · sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD) · IBM Heron processor ibm_kobe · GRPO/GSPO policy-gradient training

Abstract

Quantum hardware can provide feedback for training circuit generators beyond the reach of exact classical simulation. We train generative quantum eigensolver (GQE) policies, transformers conditioned on molecular descriptors, to generate the state-preparation circuits for sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD). Training runs first on a noiseless simulator and then with the IBM Heron processor ibm_kobe inside the loop, at 46 and 70 qubits (1.2 ×10⁸ shots for the four main training runs). A classical CCSD(T) reference energy of the training molecules enters only an admission gate and two auxiliary reward terms. During hardware training, a reward penalty prevents collapse to circuits that sample only the Hartree-Fock determinant. Policies trained on transition-metal complexes are applied without retraining to Sn(OH)₃-Me and its hydrates, minimal models of organotin photoresists for extreme-ultraviolet lithography, from 32 to 70 qubits. After one round of hardware sampling, followed by classical ranking and recovery of the cached counts with the molecular Hamiltonian and no further QPU calls, 27 of 28 runs at 46-70 qubits are within 15 mHa of the density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) reference (median 4.5 mHa), and in all eight runs with an untrained control the trained policy is more accurate. At 56-70 qubits the selected circuits use 34-72 times fewer two-qubit gates than the local unitary cluster Jastrow (LUCJ) circuit transpiled for the same device. These results demonstrate that circuit generators can be trained with quantum hardware at 70 qubits.

item.arxave:abstract: Quantum hardware can provide feedback for training circuit generators beyond the reach of exact classical simulation. We train generative quantum eigensolver (GQE) policies, transformers conditioned on molecular descriptors, to generate the state-preparation circuits for sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD). Training runs first on a noiseless simulator and then with the IBM Heron processor ibm_kobe inside the loop, at 46 and 70 qubits (1.2 ×10⁸ shots for the four main training runs). A classical CCSD(T) reference energy of the training molecules enters only an admission gate and two auxiliary reward terms. During hardware training, a reward penalty prevents collapse to circuits that sample only the Hartree-Fock determinant. Policies trained on transition-metal complexes are applied without retraining to Sn(OH)₃-Me and its hydrates, minimal models of organotin photoresists for extreme-ultraviolet lithography, from 32 to 70 qubits. After one round of hardware sampling, followed by classical ranking and recovery of the cached counts with the molecular Hamiltonian and no further QPU calls, 27 of 28 runs at 46-70 qubits are within 15 mHa of the density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) reference (median 4.5 mHa), and in all eight runs with an untrained control the trained policy is more accurate. At 56-70 qubits the selected circuits use 34-72 times fewer two-qubit gates than the local unitary cluster Jastrow (LUCJ) circuit transpiled for the same device. These results demonstrate that circuit generators can be trained with quantum hardware at 70 qubits.

item.title: Study of the frustrated SU(3) Heisenberg chain with SU(3)-symmetric matrix product states
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Trimerized valence-bond solid phase extends to αc2≳3.5 and terminates below α≈5, ruling out lower boundary around α≈2. Large-α effective central charge is consistent with massless flow from SU(3)2 to SU(3)1.

Grade 0.336 · 1.7σ above the day's baseline · matched “The density-matrix renormalization group in the age of matrix product states” · O. R. Hryniv, I. V. Lukin, A. G. Sotnikov

Asks

Where does the trimerized phase terminate in the frustrated SU(3) Heisenberg chain as a function of α=J2/J1?

Before

Estimates for upper boundary ranged from α≈2.1 via exact diagonalization to α≈3.8 via iDMRG.

But

1D chain at zero temperature; virtual bond dimension up to D≈8000.

Tools

variational uniform matrix product states (VUMPS) · non-Abelian SU(3) symmetry · finite-entanglement scaling · transfer-matrix and entanglement spectra resolution

Abstract

We study the SU(3) Heisenberg chain with nearest- and next-nearest-neighbor antiferromagnetic exchange J₁ and J₂. Field theory predicts that the trimerized valence-bond solid of this chain has a finite extent in α=J₂/J₁, followed by a gapless SU(3)₁ phase, but earlier numerical estimates of the upper boundary range from α≈2.1 (exact diagonalization) to α≈3.8 (iDMRG). We use the variational uniform matrix product state (VUMPS) algorithm with the full non-Abelian SU(3) symmetry imposed on the virtual bonds, reaching bond dimensions up to D≈8000, and locate the phase boundaries by finite-entanglement scaling. Resolving the transfer-matrix spectrum and the entanglement spectrum by SU(3) irreducible representation, we find that the trimerized phase extends to α_c2gtrsim3.5 and end below α≈5, excluding a boundary near α≈2. At larger α our numerical analysis of the effective central charge is consistent with the predicted massless flow from SU(3)₂ to SU(3)₁.

item.title: Nonperturbative string dynamics in a (2+1)D lattice gauge theory on a superconducting quantum processor
item.description:
Worth a look new result — Simulated nonperturbative flux-string dynamics in a (2+1)D ℤ2 lattice gauge theory with dynamical matter and plaquette terms for up to 15 Trotter steps (t=4.5 in units of Jv). Spatially resolved measurements show rapid charge and flux spreading in deconfined regimes, matter creation inside the string near resonance (hz/Jv=2.00), and suppressed spreading at large electric fields (hz/Jv=4.00).

Grade 0.330 · 1.6σ above the day's baseline · matched “Evidence for the utility of quantum computing before fault tolerance” · Sanziana Stelea, Anthony Gandon, Francesco Tacchino, Jad C. Halimeh, Ivano Tavernelli

Figure

Measured string-path projector values versus Trotter evolution time across different electric-field regimes (hz/Jv). Traces contrast string persistence and transverse oscillations at strong electric field (hz=4) against rapid delocalization in the deconfined phase (hz=0). direct quantum data match classical approximations.

Asks

Can quantum processors simulate the real-time, nonperturbative dynamics and transverse fluctuations of electric flux strings in a (2+1)D lattice gauge theory while exploiting gauge redundancy for error detection?

But

Restricted to diagonal local observables and string-like projectors via marginal distributions to manage exponential post-selection sampling overhead; limited to total evolution time t=4.5 (dt=0.3).

Tools

ibm_phoenix superconducting processor (63 qubits) · second-order Trotter circuit (depth-8 CNOT per step) · local Gauss-law and ancilla post-selection · Clifford perturbation theory noise rescaling · Pauli twirling

Abstract

Electric flux strings underpin confinement in gauge theories. In two spatial dimensions, their evolution involves competing processes of charge motion, pair creation, and transverse deformation. Accessing these dynamics beyond perturbative limits challenges classical approaches, as entanglement growth restricts the times accessible to tensor-network simulations. Here we use quantum simulation to investigate a (2+1)D Z2 lattice gauge theory with dynamical matter and an explicit magnetic plaquette interaction, spanning strongly confined and nonperturbative deconfined regimes. Using 63 superconducting qubits, including 12 ancillas, we evolve initially localized strings with static or dynamical endpoint charges. Spatially resolved measurements reveal rapid charge and flux spreading in the deconfined regime, enhanced matter occupation in the string interior near the pair-creation resonance, and suppressed spreading at strong electric fields. String-path occupations further probe transverse rearrangements between configurations connected by plaquette operations. Retaining separate matter and gauge degrees of freedom makes local Gauss-law constraints directly accessible for error detection. Combining these constraints with ancilla checks and noise rescaling, we measure dynamics in circuits containing up to 15 second-order Trotter steps. Our results establish quantum simulation as a practical approach to exploring nonperturbative string dynamics in two spatial dimensions, with gauge redundancy serving as an experimental resource.
